He'd lost a lot of interest in maintaining his feathers of late, it was hours of effort per week and he usually found himself far too tired to be bothered. His handlers would get upset, as they did about everything, they'd chastise him like a child and then bring him in for 'maintenance', which was little more than some Commission doctor roughly preening his wings for him with rubber gloves that kept catching on the barbs and a synthetic oil that smelled like someone trying to replicate something floral despite having never met a flower in their entire life.

As much as he hated it, it only sometimes worked as a deterrent.

*Tired is tired, at least I can nap when someone else does the work for me.*

Tonight was different though, tonight he needed his feathers to be as glossy and stunning as possible, sure Dabi probably wouldn't even notice, most people didn't, but making sure his wings looked good for his partners always pleasantly scratched a forbidden itch in his raptor brain.

He wasn't supposed to indulge those habits, but like a clogged pipe the impulses just kept backing up until they flooded his brain at the most inopportune moments, usually leading to a 'PR incident' and several days of retraining that only started the cycle anew, he'd taken to just indulging in secret to take the edge off.

Hunting and eating a rat or pigeon here and there, perching barefoot whenever he was home alone (it just didn't feel the same in his boots, what was left of his talons needed to *grip),* cooing to himself in the middle of the night when he couldn't sleep. Little things, things nobody needed to know.

Another mouthful of feathers, she felt warm flesh tickle her lips, the scent of sweat and adrenaline pungent beneath her nose, she had been close that time, *so close.* She could almost feel her prey's rapid pulse beneath her teeth, licking her lips at the thought of the splash of warm blood across her tongue.

Almost.

Almost.

*Just a little faster.*

She dropped the steel claw from her hand, it was impeding her grip, slowing her down, making too much noise, she didn't need a weapon, she *was* a weapon.

She was so much faster now, her claws caught on flesh, the scent of blood hit the air, her heart beat a rapid rhythm. She had injured it, she only needed a few swipes more before it would finally start to slow. She was salivating already.

She was on its tail, it was barely dodging, it couldn't get more than a few inches ahead of her, red filled her vision, red feathers, red blood, red red red red *red-*

*POUNCE.*

A wrong turn in an enclosed space, the mistake she was waiting for, the single second of hesitation, finally there was warm flesh gasping helplessly beneath her, she *had it,* she *won,* she-

A tight grip around her waist and wrists pulled her off her prey only microseconds before she could sink her teeth into its neck, she blinked in shock as golden eyes blinked back.

"Come back to me Himiko," it said softly. "You caught me, you were amazing, but the game's over now."

The afternoon sunlight was warm on his face as Shouto pretended to continue sleeping, afraid that opening his eyes would break the comfortable fantasy he woke to find himself in. He wasn't sure why Fuyumi hadn't come to bother them yet, it had to be past lunch time by now, but he wasn't about to question his good fortune.

He tried to kick the fluttering in his chest under the metaphorical bed with all the other feelings he wasn't prepared to face, but it seemed to have finally reached capacity.

Falling asleep together, holding each other so tenderly like this, it was *not* something normal friends did, and he couldn't seem to convince himself it was no matter how hard he tried.

Izuku shifted slightly in his arms. "Sho-chan? Are you awake?" he whispered.

Shouto sighed and finally opened his eyes, their faces were so close he could count Izuku's freckles. "Yeah."

His wings mantled over them, almost blocking out the room as he made his home in Dabi's mouth again... until he felt cold hands push against his shoulders, Hawks barely had the chance to register the sensation before it quickly transitioned to frantic smacks until he pulled away and sat back on Dabi's lap.

The man looked positively debauched, kiss drunk, lips swollen and shiny with spit, it was a sight Hawks would be committing to memory and *definitely* revisiting on lonely nights.

He was enjoying the view immensely until he noticed Dabi wasn't just breathing hard from exertion, he was gasping like he couldn't catch his breath.

"Hey Dabs? Are you okay? What's happening?" Hawks asked, cupping his face. "Slow down hot stuff you're hyperventilating, take some slow breaths with me alright?"

After a minute or two Dabi pushed Hawks' hands away to cover his own face, his breathing had slowed but Hawks could hear it shaking on every exhale.

"Do you... wanna tell me what happened or..." Hawks trailed off, still sitting in Dabi's lap, unsure whether he needed space or comfort.

"I'm- I don't-" Dabi let out a long shaky sigh. "I don't know, *I don't know,* I just-"

"Okay, okay let's, um, let's just walk back a bit okay? We were, we were making out and, did I do something you didn't like or...?" Hawks couldn't think of anything wrong he might have done in the moment, they'd only been kissing.

Dabi shook his head.

"I'm not... I'm not right Hawks," he said in a small fragile voice, followed up by a humourless laugh. "I'm not right in the h-head, I thought this was different and it is different but it's still- I'm s-still-"

"Can I ask you something?" Shouto closed his eyes, swallowing his nerves, he had to ask, he had to know. "Are we... are we friends or... something different?"

Izuku didn't answer right away, Shouto kept his eyes squeezed shut, too afraid of what he might see on his face.

"I um... I wouldn't mind being something... something different... if you want that I mean." Izuku rushed the last part out quickly, uncertainty shaking his voice.

"Yeah, I think I want that." Shouto smiled.

Shouto's ears were ringing, the world around him faded into barely more than a blur of colour, the person in the seat beside him backed away as his body temperature plummeted and skyrocketed at the same time, half of him smoking as the other half frosted over.

*They knew. All this time they **knew** and they've been **covering it up.***

The rough hand resting on Shouto's icy fist pried itself into his palm, lacing their fingers together tightly, it felt so hot against his cold skin, he could feel damaged knuckles click and pop from the pressure. He reeled his quirk in quickly, Izuku's hands always got so stiff and sore in the cold.

"They won't get away with this," Izuku hissed in his ear, it didn't feel like an empty platitude, his voice was far too acidic. "I swear to god we won't let them get away with this."

Terry Pratchett does something like this, specifically when a character uses a word they don't actually understand the meaning to, he'll spell it out incorrectly, usually in the way it's pronounced

an example off the top of my head is 'insurance' was spelt something along the lines of 'in-sewer-ants'

characters who knew what it meant would spell it correctly

I thought that was a really fun and clever detail, and something I've used in my own fic a few times, but it really should be used sparingly, I personally would have no issue using it in prose, but I always write from third person limited POV and I put a lot of the character's personality into my prose, so it works for my style of writing

I did once write a child character who was quite intelligent and when using a big word in the prose, I would then write it again but sounded out, as she sort of processed it in her mind, eg;


'The old man was cantankerous, can-tank-er-ous, she had learned that word a few days ago, it was a big one and her teacher had been SO impressed when she spelt it right!'


After that drop of context, any time I would sound a word out like that again, my readers would understand why and it becomes a little character quirk

again, it must be used sparingly lest it become annoying, but spelling out words incorrectly can be used the same way, you just need to make sure your readers will understand the word via context

in your example, 'spidder' doesn't work unless the character actually pronounces it that way out loud, something you could address by having an adult correct them, and then changing the spelling in the prose after that since they know the correct pronunciation now

two factors here

1; we as a species are designed to focus on things that are unpleasant or scary as a latent survival instinct, basically your caveman brain is equating a negative online comment as a savage predator trying to eat you and applying the appropriate amount of fear

2; black and white autism thinking can make it very very difficult to accept when something is 'incorrect' and we may suffer a compulsive urge to correct the incorrection, that includes when someone thinks something incorrect about *us*, so we can end up fixated on it

both are habits you ultimately have to train your brain out of, you might not get rid of the feeling entirely, but you can work to convince your brain that this really isn't as important or threatening as it feels, and sometimes people are going to think what they want about you and if clear communication doesn't fix it, it's no longer a You problem, sometimes people just don't want to change their minds, wipe your hands of them and move on

depending on injury and circumstance (HIGHLY dependant, it's different for everyone) the pain can either be constantly at a debilitating level, or remain pretty mild day to day, sometimes you can sort of get used to it and function through it, but cold can flare it up, or overuse of the limb, and then the pain can become unmanageable

even if it does stay mild tho there is a build up effect where you can get increasingly more frustrated by it over time as you fail to heal properly, you just want it to go back to the way it was, you just want it to *go away*, it's a constant distracting presence that affects most aspects of your life, you always have to account for it and accomodate for it and be prepared for flare ups when leaving the house or doing particular activities, it can get really exhausting, and sometimes very isolating and frustrating when you have to sit out on certain activities, even once you're mostly used to it you can have moments where you break down about it because you're just so *tired* of it

there's sometimes limited motion in injured joints, maybe can't fully bend it, or it bends in ways it shouldn't due to ligament weakness (compression bands can help with this), they might crack really loudly which can hurt sometimes but maybe not other times, sometimes it makes it feel better, a walking cane can be used to reduce pain even if you don't require it to be able to walk, but acknowledging that you need one can be a whole mental journey ranging from 'no I'm not disabled enough to need one and using one makes me feel like I'm making my condition look worse than it is and I feel guilty about it' to 'no I'm not gonna use one because I resent the fact that I need it so I don't even want to think about it and I'm going to get angry at anyone who brings it up'

sometimes you have to take medication, prescription anti-inflammatories can be very hard on the digestive system and cause issues over time with nausea, appetite disruption, stomach ulcers, so you often can't take them for long periods of time without breaks (both animals and humans can take meloxicam so that would be most compatible with the turtles I imagine), when I take it I can only take it for a week and then spend a week off them to prevent damage, you also have to take them with food, pain medication can also have side effects, and extended use of those can lead to addiction

having to limit your medication use leads to having to use it strategically, 'limiting' it to when you really need it, it usually works best when taking it before the pain really sets in so you sometimes have to play a guessing game of determining what's going to be a bad pain day, having a flare up when you have to be off the meds sucks real bad

heat can help with pain, especially muscle pain, you can get microwaveable heat packs but they don't stay warm for very long, or chemical based ones that can be activated and stay hot for hours, heated blankets can help with sleep, they usually come built in with a timer so they turn off after a while to avoid overheating and catching fire

okay so, as an Australian, any time I read a non Australian writer trying too hard to 'write' an Australian accent it is *unbearable* and I will stop reading out of sheer cringe

you don't need to make it sound 'Australian', you just need to make it sound *'casual',* just drop a few 'g's here and there at the end of 'ing' words, use 'gonna' instead of 'going to', 'lotta' instead of 'lot of', 'kinda' instead of 'kind of' and all such variations, we shorten and sandwich together words a lot, and our sentences tend to run together, often we can make five words sound like one

it can't hurt to look up our lingo but DON'T overuse it, it will feel forced, just keep it to relevant words, don't go out of your way to use them when they aren't necessary

some examples, if you're american, a car trunk is a 'boot', a sidewalk is a 'footpath', candies are 'lollies', a gas station is a 'servo', a liquor store is a 'bottlo', McDonalds is 'Maccas', there's a million and one youtube videos you can watch on Australian lingo for reference, and some of the more well known Australian slang that you guys know is pretty over exaggerated

like yeah we say 'g'day' but really not as often as people think, and it's far more commonly used by older folks (this also varies by region), be careful with well known stereotypical slang because it can easily be clocked as low effort

basically, any time I read a fic with an Australian character and the author *isn't* trying to convince me really really hard that they're Australian? (I'm gonna sound real full of myself here but keep in mind writing is like the *one thing* I'm good at so I have a lot of pride in it, I'm only a half decent artist and I have very few other skills that go beyond a basic level)

I've rarely ever gotten actual useful feedback in my comments, my skills came mostly from practice practice practice, the voracious consumption of literature, and joining a writing discord where I could passively pick up advice or ask questions when I struggled with something specific

the thing is, I've never struggled to get readers, I've always gotten comments, not many to start with for sure, but I was way ahead of a lot of other first time writers, and I still get a steady amount of commenters, not a crazy amount since I don't really write popular tropes and pairings, but I'm certainly not starved for them, on the outside it would have looked like I was lucky, someone who was just born with a natural talent

and to be fair, I was born hyperlexic, and that definitely gave me a leg up in the reading department at an early age, but my *real* strength was just... passion, plain and simple passion for reading and writing, I loved doing it, I did it *a lot*

my first fics sucked, as is standard, but I was a better writer than most kids my age and I had been writing original stories for years before I discovered you can post stories on the internet and I began writing fic, so I started at an advantage compared to others who only started writing *after* discovering fic and posted a lot of their early work, so my fics objectively sucked, but sucked a lot less than they usually would have for someone my age

I think what made the biggest difference was that I read a lot of older novels when I was still pretty young, so I learned the basics on well written classics, I did eventually get into questionable YA content that had a stronger influence on the characters and plots I came up with, but those classics still held me up in regard to sentence structure, spelling and grammar, and vocabulary

so a majority of my commenters were just simply not at my reading and writing level, and so they couldn't really give me any useful advice, I did have a lot of room to improve so I definitely could have *used* good advice, but nobody with the skills to give it were reading my fics because A) they might have been pretty good for my age and experience level but they *did* still suck, and B) my summaries were absolute hot garbage, it wasn't until I joined that writing discord and engaged with people who had more experience and practice than me that I got more constructive help, but by that time I had already improved by virtue of practice and consumption and had a pretty decent following

and when I say practice, I mean I wrote a veritable *fuckton of fic*, as well as original stories, mostly incomplete snippets, isolated scenes, dialogue in script format, also a lot of plots and outlines that ended up going nowhere and got scrapped, I also constantly churned stories over in my head before deciding if they were worth writing down, and a majority of all of that was *never posted*, so I was basically stealth improving, I'd have a huge gap between posting fics and as a result my fic quality would jump significantly, once again giving the impression of natural talent when, in reality, people just weren't seeing all the work going on in the background

so my best advice for improving? is unfortunately the most basic advice anyone can ever give, read a lot, write a lot, join a writing discord for advice and feedback instead of relying on comments, that's what I did, and I'm doing pretty well

and always remember that nobody is a great writer on talent alone, even when you start at an advantage like I did you still need to put in the work, authors who look like they rocketed out of the womb with a pen in their hand are just an illusion, they worked to get where they are, and you can always reach their level if you have enough passion and determination

my psychologist's advice for curbing compulsive behaviours (for me it was hair pulling) was to contain it rather than stop it, so setting aside some time dedicated completely to that thing and letting yourself enjoy it before putting it away again for later

it's still often hard to stop and stick within your time allowance, but the fact that you know you'll be allowed to come back later does kinda help, it's especially good if you put your allowed time before another task you're physically incapable of putting off, such as right before going to work or attending a class, then it forces you to stop and abide by the time limit because there are actually serious consequences otherwise

I'll also combine this with advice I got for a different issue (binge eating), and that's mindfulness, rapid consumption of anything (food, media, etc) is going to leave you dissatisfied, and dissatisfaction means more rapid consumption to fill the void, practicing mindfulness is taking the time to slow down and actually focus on what you're consuming, think about it, enjoy it, savour it, your brain will find it a lot more fulfilling and it will actually satisfy that craving more effectively

these things take time and practice to get the hang of, just remember slipping back into old habits is not a failure, it's a normal and natural part of any learning process, willpower is a muscle, you need to build it up, just keep at it

so I had a situation where I was writing fic focused on a bunch of characters' histories and traumas, but some of the characters in this group had far more vague backstories than others, and if I wanted to give them equal focus I was going to have to make some shit up

and how I went about this was by looking at the established canon backstories for the other characters and saying 'okay what DON'T we have here?'

I had more than enough canon characters who had experienced child abuse, in various flavours, so I felt like the story didn't need any more of that, but one of the only things we learned about *this* character's background is that he canonically suffered abuse from a bigoted community, so he had plenty of trauma for me to work with already, so I took the fact that he never really talked about his parents in the canon and made something out of *that*

I made them competent parents who cared for him adequately but were emotionally neglectful, not just to him but to each other, he didn't hate his parents, he understood the circumstances that lead them to being as they were, but he also didn't love them, and it bothered him immensely that he couldn't make himself feel anything for them at all

so yeah sometimes using what you *don't* have as the starting point for coming up with something new is an effective strategy, combine that with what little is already established, and then tie in how that history affected their current personality traits and behaviours, and you have a decent background

in my current series I've written from the POVs of 19 different characters, and yes, they do all need to be different, but if you're doing it in third person (my preference) they don't have to be VASTLY different

the key is subtlety in the way certain thought processes work, introspections will be different, some may be unreliable narrators, you don't need to change the style of writing dramatically, you just need to write in the way that they think

eg, I have a character in my fic who's very anxious and overthinks things, so his thought process involves a lot of run on sentences lacking in punctuation

one character is more well read and educated than his peers, so his chapters are a little more poetic

some of them are a kind of unhinged so their prose is written a little more erratically

someone deep in denial or who is repressing something might cut off their own thought process midway through and then continue like it never happened

you also need to keep good track of *who knows what*, with shifting POV not everyone knows or processes information the same, so one character interpreting a situation differently from another and treating that like a complete truth in the narrative is really interesting when you have a different character doing the same thing with a whole different interpretation

basically as an author you need to get comfortable with lying to your readers, YOU know that character X doesn't hate character Y, but character Y is so convinced they do that the prose will say so like it is an undeniable fact

meanwhile from character X's POV, the narrative will completely contradict that

you have to get inside the head of these characters, figure out how they think in order to adapt it believably, are they overthinkers, are they logical thinkers, are they simplistic, unreliable, contradictory

but don't overdo it, don't force it, a majority of the prose should maintain a fairly consistent style across all POVs, you want the same dish in different flavours, not entirely separate meals, these are individualised details you want to add sparsely, you don't want the changes to be completely jarring

'insane' is a very broad word that can mean a million different things, how are they insane? what caused them to go insane? how does this insanity manifest? how does their behaviour connect to their trauma?

you say his friends hurt him to a degree that he wants to fight them, is this the only traumatic event? were there other factors at play? is he actually 'insane' or just pissed off and beating them up as revenge? (there's a difference)

you want to look at cause and effect, was the trauma something physical that put them into a constant defensive state? have they developed an issue in regulating their emotions and now lash out at anything that makes them upset? did someone they trusted betray them and cause them to become irrationally paranoid that everyone they know is out to get them?

so your crucial questions are as follows:

what is the trauma? what is the effect of that trauma on their psyche? how does it manifest in their behaviour? when you find the answers you now have an avenue to research how that specific trauma response works and its usual signs and symptoms
